Turn this lecture transcript into structured study notes with headings, then write five exam-style questions.

Right, so today is urban heat islands. The basic observation is simple and it's been known for about two hundred years: cities are warmer than the countryside around them. On a calm clear night the centre of a large city can be five, six, sometimes ten degrees warmer than farmland twenty kilometres away. During the day the difference in air temperature is usually smaller, a degree or two, though surfaces themselves, roads and roofs, can be dramatically hotter.

Why does it happen? Four main reasons, and you should be able to list them. One, materials. Asphalt, concrete and brick absorb a lot of sunlight and store it as heat, then release it slowly after sunset. That's why the effect is strongest at night. Two, lack of vegetation and water. In the countryside a good part of the sun's energy goes into evaporating water from soil and leaves, which cools the air. Cities have sealed surfaces and drains that carry water away, so that energy heats the air instead. Three, geometry. Tall buildings on narrow streets form what we call urban canyons. They trap outgoing heat because the walls absorb what the street radiates, and they block wind. Four, waste heat from us: vehicles, air conditioners, industry. Note the nasty loop with air conditioning. The hotter it gets, the more we run it, and every unit dumps heat outside.

Why do we care? Heatwaves kill more people in many countries than storms or floods, and deaths concentrate in cities, among older people, and in poorer neighbourhoods, which tend to have fewer trees. There's energy demand, which peaks exactly when the grid is most stressed. And there's air quality, because some pollutants form faster in heat.

What can be done? Three families of measures. Increase reflectivity: light-coloured roofs and pavements, which are cheap but can cause glare and do little at night. Increase vegetation: street trees, parks, green roofs. Trees are the most effective per dollar where there's room and water, but they take a decade to mature and need maintenance. And reduce waste heat through efficiency and better building design. No single one is enough.

A common confusion for the exam: the urban heat island is not the same thing as global warming. It's a local effect caused by land use. But the two add together, which is why cities are where warming will be felt first and hardest.

I wrote this comparison for our team blog but it rambles. Turn it into a pros/cons table for each option plus a two-sentence recommendation that matches what I actually concluded.

We spent the last month trialling three ways of handling background jobs in our app, because the current setup (cron scripts on one server) has let us down twice this year.

The first option was to keep cron but make it less fragile: move the scripts into the main codebase, add locking so jobs can't overlap, and send failures to our alerting. This took two days. It's familiar and there's nothing new to run. But it doesn't solve the real problem, which is that everything still depends on one machine, and there's still no way to retry a single failed item without rerunning the whole script. When the nightly invoice run failed halfway in March, we had to work out by hand which customers had been billed.

The second option was a database-backed job queue, using a library that stores jobs in a table in the Postgres database we already have. Workers poll the table. This took about a week to trial properly. I liked it more than I expected. Jobs are transactional with our data, so we can enqueue a 'send receipt' job in the same transaction that records the payment and never get one without the other. Retries and a dead-letter list come for free. We can see the queue with plain SQL. The downsides: polling adds a little load to the database, throughput tops out somewhere around a few hundred jobs per second in our test, which is far more than we need today but not infinite, and the library is maintained by a small team.

The third option was a dedicated message broker with a separate worker framework. This is what the bigger companies do and it's what two of our engineers have used before. Throughput was excellent, tens of thousands of jobs per second. It has scheduling, priorities, rate limits, a dashboard. But it's a new piece of infrastructure to run, monitor, upgrade and secure, and we're a team of five with no dedicated operations person. We also lose the transactional enqueue, so we'd need the outbox pattern to avoid lost or phantom jobs, which is more code and more ways to get it wrong. In the trial we hit a confusing issue with jobs running twice after a worker restart that took a day to understand.

Where I landed: the broker is the better tool, but the database queue is the better fit for us right now. We process maybe 20,000 jobs a day. If we grow by a factor of fifty I'll happily revisit this, and migrating from one to the other is not a one-way door because the job code itself barely changes.

From these release notes, produce a migration checklist for someone upgrading from 2.x to 3.0, ordered so that each step can be verified before the next.

formkit-validate 3.0.0 release notes

This is a major release. It removes APIs deprecated during the 2.x series, changes some defaults and raises minimum requirements.

Requirements. Node 18 is no longer supported; the minimum is Node 20. The package is now published as ES modules only. CommonJS consumers must use dynamic import or stay on 2.x, which will receive security fixes until the end of next June.

Removed. The validateSync function has been removed; use validate, which now returns synchronously when no asynchronous rules are present and a promise otherwise. The legacy string rule syntax ('required|min:3') was deprecated in 2.4 and is now removed; use the rule builder functions. The global addRule function is removed in favour of passing custom rules to createValidator.

Changed defaults. Unknown fields in the input are now rejected by default; previously they were silently stripped. To restore the old behaviour pass unknownFields: 'strip'. Empty strings are no longer treated as missing for required fields unless trimEmpty is true. Error messages are now returned as objects with code, path and message properties rather than plain strings; a toStrings helper is provided for a quick migration.

Renamed. The option abortEarly is now called stopOnFirstError. The old name is accepted with a console warning in 3.0 and will be removed in 3.1. The min and max rules for strings have been renamed minLength and maxLength; min and max now apply only to numbers and dates and will throw if used on a string field.

New. Schemas can be composed with extend and pick. Async rules can declare a debounce interval. TypeScript types for the validated output are now inferred from the schema; the manual generic parameter on validate is no longer needed and has been removed.

Fixed. Date rules now compare in UTC consistently. Nested array paths in errors are reported with numeric indexes (items.2.name) instead of bracket syntax.

Codemod. A codemod is available that rewrites the string rule syntax and the renamed options automatically. It does not handle the error object change or custom rules registered with addRule.

Known issues. Type inference is slow on schemas with more than about 200 fields.
